Arts. 13-14 (equality of rights; equal labour rights)

answers.implementation_then_now: Neither date has any practice evidence of foreign workers with valid permits being denied enrolment in contributory schemes (AFP pensions, health, workplace accident insurance) on grounds of nationality. The ISL states that its work-accident insurance covers everyone who works in Chile 'sin importar su nacionalidad'. Fully state-funded benefits reach migrants once they meet the residence conditions: a Qualimet study for the Consejo Consultivo Previsional (reported April 2026) counted 13,464 foreign PGU recipients in 2022 and about US$60m of PGU spending on migrants projected for 2025. There are known gaps: high informality among recently arrived migrants means no contributions are paid, and some PGU claims are rejected because residence cannot be proved. These are mostly not refusals of the legal right to permit holders. I found no evidence of a shift between 2023 and 2026, so the starting rating is kept for both dates.

answers.sourcing_note: I read the LeyChile JSON for Ley 21.325 in both the current version (from 2026-06-02) and the original version in force from 2022-02-12 to 2023-08-06. Art. 16 has the same text in both, and no amendment notes appear on Arts. 13-16. The version list shows changes on 2023-08-07, 2023-08-18, 2023-09-22, 2024-02-20 (Ley 21.655), 2025-04-01 and 2026-06-02, all to other articles. I could not open the practice studies themselves (the Previsión Social/Qualimet PDF and the Mirada FEN PDF); I relied on the press report.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The starting citation says the law covers 'some, but not all types' of protection, yet the answer chosen is 'after some period of time'. Under Art. 16, contributory benefits are equal from the start, the 24-month residence rule applies only to fully state-funded non-contributory cash transfers, and specific laws such as the PGU require 20 years of residence. That fits either the 75 or the 50 option. 'Effectively Always' is also generous given documented informality and PGU rejections for unproven residence; 'Usually' would be more defensible. I have kept the starting answers, since no dated event changes them.
answers.notes: The provision is statutory (Ley 21.325 Art. 16), confirmed against the version history; no court decision was relied on. Ley 21.735 (pension reform, D.O. 26.03.2025) created new contributory benefits that do not depend on nationality. I did not establish whether it changed the PGU residence requirement; ChileAtiende's current PGU page still lists the 20-year/4-of-5-years residence rule.

answers.implementation_then_now: Membership of the Seguro de Cesantía is automatic for every dependent worker under the Código del Trabajo. The ChileAtiende eligibility page lists no nationality condition, and I found no documented refusals of the insurance to foreign workers with valid permits in either period. Press reports and academic work using ENE data (search snippets only; the Mirada FEN PDF and the DF article could not be opened) suggest migrants with formal contracts pay into the insurance at least as often as nationals. The main gap is informality, which affects migrants without permits more than permit holders. I found no evidence of a shift between 2023 and 2026, so the rating is unchanged.
answers.sourcing_note: I read the LeyChile JSON for Ley 19.728. Art. 1 has no amendment notes, and its version list covers 2020-10-01 to 2023-11-30 and later versions up to 2026-06-01. The amendments I saw in the window (Ley 21.628, Ley 21.735) do not concern nationality. Arts. 13-14 of Ley 21.325 have the same text in the original (2022-02-12) and current versions. No direct practice source on foreign beneficiaries of the unemployment insurance could be opened.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Access is equal in law, but every claimant, national or foreign, must first have paid a minimum number of contributions (now 10). 'Immediate' therefore means no nationality or residence condition, not benefits from the first day. 'Effectively Always' rests on no direct evidence about practice; given the documented informality among migrants, 'Usually' may be more defensible.
answers.notes: The protection rests on statute (Ley 19.728 Art. 1, which covers all dependent workers under the Código del Trabajo, and Ley 21.325 Arts. 13-14 on equal labour rights); no court decision was relied on. Confidence is low because I found no source on actual practice for foreign claimants in either period.
